study.title: When Israel departed from Egypt
study.intro: Psalm 114 is a short, vivid poem about the exodus. In just eight verses it pictures the Red Sea fleeing, the Jordan River turning back and the mountains skipping like young sheep, all because God was present with His people. It ends by calling the whole earth to tremble before the God who turns rock into water.
study.context: Psalm 114 is the second psalm of the Egyptian Hallel and was sung before the Passover meal. It compresses Israel's journey from Egypt to the promised land: the Red Sea crossing (Exodus 14), the shaking of Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:18), water from the rock (Exodus 17 and Numbers 20) and the Jordan crossing (Joshua 3). It treats nature itself as a witness responding to God.
study.peopleNote: The psalm names Israel, Jacob and Judah as God's people. It recalls the exodus led by Moses, though he is not named. God is never portrayed as a human figure in planned art; His presence is shown through parted waters and shaking hills.

verses.title: Out of Egypt
verses.heading: The house of Jacob departed
verses.meaning: 'When Israel departed from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of foreign tongue,' The psalm starts with the founding event of Israel's story. They had been slaves in a land whose language was strange to them. God brought them out. Every Passover, Israel remembered that their freedom did not come from their own strength, but from God's mighty rescue.
verses.context: Exodus 12-14 tells how God brought Israel out of Egypt. 'House of Jacob' recalls that the nation came from Jacob's family, who went down to Egypt in Genesis 46.
explore: House of Jacob
The family and descendants of Jacob, also called Israel, who became the nation.
Foreign tongue
A language the Israelites did not understand, marking Egypt as a place where they were strangers.
verses.reflect: What has God brought you out of that you want to remember with thanks?
verses.alt: A long line of families with donkeys leaving a river city at dawn.

verses.title: God's own dwelling
verses.heading: Judah became God's sanctuary
verses.meaning: 'Judah became God's sanctuary, Israel His dominion.' The purpose of the exodus was not just escape. God freed His people to live with them. The whole nation became His holy place and His kingdom. They belonged to Him, and He made His home among them. Freedom from slavery led to a new life in God's presence.
verses.context: At Sinai God told Israel they would be 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation' (Exodus 19:6). Peter applies these words to believers in 1 Peter 2:9.
explore: Sanctuary
A holy place set apart where God dwells and is worshiped.
Dominion
The realm a king rules over; the people under his reign.
verses.reflect: How does knowing you were rescued to belong to God shape the way you live?
verses.alt: A tent camp surrounding a central tent under a pillar of cloud.

verses.title: Sea and river retreat
verses.heading: The sea observed and fled
verses.meaning: 'The sea observed and fled; the Jordan turned back;' The poem treats the waters like living creatures. The Red Sea saw God coming and ran away. Forty years later the Jordan River backed up so Israel could cross. The two water crossings frame the whole journey, the first at the start leaving Egypt and the second at the end entering the land.
verses.context: Exodus 14:21-22 tells of the Red Sea parting, and Joshua 3:14-17 tells how the Jordan stopped flowing when the priests stepped in with the ark.
explore: Observed
Saw and took notice; the poem pictures the sea as aware of God's presence.
Jordan
The river at the eastern edge of the promised land, crossed by Israel under Joshua.
verses.reflect: What obstacle in your path seems as fixed as a sea or river?
verses.alt: Walls of water standing on either side of a dry seabed path.

verses.title: Skipping mountains
verses.heading: Like rams and lambs
verses.meaning: 'the mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs.' The great mountains, which seem so solid and permanent, are pictured jumping like young sheep. This likely recalls Mount Sinai quaking when God came down. The image is almost playful. What people fear as immovable is as light as a lamb before the Creator.
verses.context: Exodus 19:18 says the whole mountain of Sinai trembled violently when the LORD descended on it. Psalm 29:6 also says God makes Lebanon skip like a calf.
explore: Rams
Male sheep, strong and lively, known for leaping on rocky slopes.
Hills like lambs
Smaller heights pictured as young sheep bounding about in the field.
verses.reflect: What problem looks like a mountain to you but is small before God?
verses.alt: Lambs leaping across a grassy hillside below rugged peaks.

verses.title: A question for the waters
verses.heading: Why was it, O sea
verses.meaning: 'Why was it, O sea, that you fled, O Jordan, that you turned back,' Now the singer speaks directly to the sea and the river, teasingly asking what made them run. The answer is obvious, but holding it back builds suspense. The question invites everyone singing to supply the answer in their hearts: it was the presence of God.
verses.context: Asking creation questions is a way of drawing listeners in. Habakkuk 3:8 asks a similar question: 'Were You angry at the rivers, O LORD?' Both poets expect the listener to know the answer.
explore: Fled
Ran away in haste, as an army or a frightened animal flees.
Turned back
Reversed its normal flow, as the Jordan did when it stopped upstream.
verses.reflect: If someone asked what changed your life's direction, what would you want your answer to be?
verses.alt: A riverbed with water halted upstream and stones exposed.

verses.title: A question for the hills
verses.heading: O mountains, that you skipped
verses.meaning: 'O mountains, that you skipped like rams, O hills, like lambs?' The question continues to the mountains and hills. Repeating the earlier picture makes the moment linger, a little like a refrain in a song. The audience is waiting for the answer, and the very next verse will deliver that answer with real power and awe.
verses.context: Hebrew poetry often repeats a line with slight variation. Verse 6 mirrors verse 4 exactly to build up to the climax in verse 7, where the answer finally comes.
explore: Refrain
A repeated line or picture in a song that helps listeners remember and join in.
Climax
The high point of a poem or story, where tension built up is released.
verses.reflect: Which picture in this psalm helps you most to remember God's power?
verses.alt: Rolling hills under a bright sky with sheep scattered across them.

verses.title: Earth, tremble
verses.heading: At the presence of the Lord
verses.meaning: 'Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob,' Here is the answer: the sea, river and mountains moved because the Lord was present. Now the whole earth is told to tremble before Him. Yet He is called 'the God of Jacob', the God of a flawed, wandering man. His overwhelming power is joined to faithful, personal care for His people.
verses.context: Psalm 46:7 calls 'the God of Jacob' our fortress. Jacob was a deceiver God transformed, showing that God's power serves His mercy toward ordinary, imperfect people.
explore: Tremble
Shake with awe, as the ground shakes in an earthquake.
Presence
God's face or nearness; where He is actively with His people.
verses.reflect: How can you hold together awe at God's power and comfort in His closeness?
verses.alt: Dust rising from shaking ground as villagers look up in awe.

verses.title: Rock into fountain
verses.heading: The flint into a fountain
verses.meaning: 'who turned the rock into a pool, the flint into a fountain of water!' The psalm ends with a gentle miracle after the shaking ones. In the desert, God made water flow from hard rock so His thirsty people could drink. The God who makes mountains tremble also provides for His people's thirst. Paul saw in that rock a picture of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4).
verses.context: Exodus 17:6 and Numbers 20:11 tell of water flowing from rock in the wilderness. 1 Corinthians 10:4 says, 'that rock was Christ.' Jesus also offers living water (John 4:14).
explore: Flint
Very hard stone, the least likely source of water imaginable.
Fountain
A spring of water that keeps flowing, giving life in a dry place.
verses.reflect: Where in your life do you need God to bring water out of something hard?
verses.alt: Clear water pouring from a cleft in a desert rock into a pool.
